<explanation>
Below is a step‐by‐step explanation on how to create a detailed system design diagram for wttr.in, tailored specifically to its purpose as a console-oriented weather forecast service (supporting ANSI/HTML/PNG/JSON/Prometheus outputs) and its mixed-language (Go and Python) modular architecture.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
 • wttr.in is a weather forecasting service that parses external weather data (via wego and third‐party APIs) and delivers multiple output formats in a console-friendly way. Its README and file layout indicate it supports several display formats (ANSI for terminal, PNG images, HTML, JSON, etc.) and integrates geolocation, weather processing, and formatting features.
 • The service is accessed directly through URL queries (with parameters for location, format, etc.) and optionally sits behind a proxy/web server (e.g. nginx) as described.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
 • Top-level files like Dockerfile, Makefile, and configuration files (config/) indicate that the project is containerizable and deployable.
 • The presence of a go.mod/go.sum and an extensive /internal directory (with packages such as config, geo, processor, routing, view, logging, etc.) shows that a large portion of the logic is implemented in Go.
 • The /bin directory contains executable scripts (e.g. geo-proxy.py, proxy.py, srv.py) that serve as entry-points or utilities.
 • The /lib directory contains Python modules for additional functionality (such as formatting, translations, and caching), suggesting a role as helper libraries.
 • The /share directory holds static assets, translations, templates, sample systemd units, and Docker-related artifacts which are used during deployment and as reference assets.

3. Extract Key Architectural Insights from the README:
 • The README explains various client use cases (curl command examples, browser usage, integration into tmux, WeeChat, etc.) and detailed steps for installation and configuration. This tells you that the architecture must support lightweight, fast responses for high query volumes.
 • It outlines multiple output formats and customization options, so the view layer (under /internal/view and /lib/view) must be a key component.
 • The integration with external dependencies (wego, geoip2, etc.) emphasizes that the system interfaces with external APIs and databases (e.g., GeoLite2, IP2Location).

4. Outline the Main Components for Your Diagram:
 a. External Clients & Gateways:
  – Users (via CLI, web browsers, or integrated tools like tmux/WeeChat) sending HTTP requests.
  – Optionally, a reverse proxy (e.g. nginx as described in the installation docs) that forwards requests to the service.
 b. Core Service / Application Layer:
  – HTTP Server Component: This is run by one of the entry point scripts (srv.py in /bin or the Go-based binary), handling incoming HTTP requests.
  – Routing Module: Located in /internal/routing, it directs incoming queries to appropriate handling modules.
  – View Formatting Modules: Found in /internal/view (v1, with additional modules in /lib/view), responsible for rendering responses in ANSI, HTML, PNG, JSON, etc.
  – Processing Modules: The /internal/processor package deals with weather data processing (e.g., handling peaks, conversion logic).
  – Geo and Location Services: Modules under /internal/geo (with subdirectories for ip and location) manage geolocation lookups, including IP-based location, special location queries, and caching (as seen in cache.go).
  – Configuration & Logging Modules: /internal/config and /internal/logging serve to initialize configurations and log messages, ensuring proper observability and error reporting.
  – Auxiliary Utilities: Helper libraries in /internal/util (for file, HTTP, YAML operations) and Python-based libraries in /lib support additional functionality.
 c. Data & External Dependencies:
  – Weather API Integration: Uses “wego” (a Go-based weather client) which retrieves weather data from WorldWeatherOnline.
  – External Geolocation Services: Integration with free (GeoLite2) and optionally paid (IP2Location) geolocation databases.
  – Miscellaneous: Additional assets like translations, static images/assets, and system scripts reside in /share and help with both localization and deployment.

5. Relationships and Interactions:
 • Draw directional arrows from External Clients (CLI, Browser, etc.) to the HTTP Server layer.
 • The HTTP Server forwards requests to the Routing Module, which then queries:
  – The Geo Location Modules for determining the location (based on URL parameters or IP address).
  – The Processor which fetches and prepares weather information (likely by invoking wego or similar backends).
 • The View Formatting Modules then take the processed data and render the output in the requested format (ANSI, PNG, JSON, etc.).
 • The Logging and Config components wrap around the entire processing pipeline, ensuring appropriate error handling and configurable behavior.
 • Indicate side-chains or integration points to external services (like weather APIs and geo-databases).

6. Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
 • Layered/MVC-Like Structure: Separation between input handling (HTTP/routing), business logic (geo, processing), and presentation (view/formatter).
 • Modularization: The project is organized in modular packages in /internal and /lib; each module (geo, routing, processor, etc.) is responsible for a distinct functionality.
 • Polyglot Environment: While primarily Go is used for core modules, some Python scripts support auxiliary or legacy functions.
 • External Integration: Use of external APIs and databases is pivotal for geolocation and weather data.

7. Guidelines for Diagram Creation:
 • Clearly label each major component or module (e.g., “HTTP Server”, “Routing”, “Geo/Location Service”, “Weather Processor”, “View Renderer”, “Config & Logging”).
 • Use directional arrows to indicate request flow: from the client → server → routers → various processing modules → response render, with annotations if needed.
 • Apply color coding or different shapes to differentiate between layers (e.g., external interfaces vs. internal logic vs. auxiliary helpers).
 • Group related components together (for example, enclose all /internal modules in an “Application Core” boundary and /share or configuration files in a “Deployment & Config” zone).

8. Final Diagram Tips:
 • In the diagram, consider drawing separate boxes for External Clients/Web Proxy, the Core Application (dividing into sub-boxes for Routing, Geo Service, Processing, and View layers), and the External Dependencies (Weather APIs, Geo databases).
 • Ensure that each box has a clear label and that data flows are annotated with the type of data (e.g., “HTTP Request”, “geolocation lookup”, “weather data”).
 • Keep the design detailed but not cluttered—focus on capturing the essential architecture while grouping related functionalities.

By following this structured approach and tailoring the diagram with clear labels, directional flows, and distinct groupings, you’ll produce a comprehensive system architecture diagram that accurately reflects the inner workings and external interactions of wttr.in.
</explanation>
